analysis.one_liner: Makes big data companies tell users what their data is worth and delete it.
analysis.headline: The data-privacy bill never got a vote: after its June 2019 introduction it sat in the Senate Banking Committee, whose only action was a hearing in October 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required large online companies and data brokers — those with more than 100 million U.S. users — to tell users what types of data are collected and how it is used, give each user an estimate of what the company thinks their data is worth, and let users delete their data with a single setting. It would have also required companies whose stock is publicly traded to disclose the value of the user data they hold and the deals they make with third parties to collect it. The Federal Trade Commission would enforce the user-facing rules and the Securities and Exchange Commission would set the investor-disclosure rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Users of the largest online platforms and data brokers — hundreds of millions of Americans — who would learn what data is collected about them, how it is used, and what the company considers it worth, and could delete it. Investors would also get standardized disclosure of how much revenue a company derives from user data.

how_it_helps.text: Every 90 days, companies with over 100 million U.S. users would have to tell each user what data is collected, how it is used beyond the service itself, and the economic value the company places on that user's data.
Users would get a single setting or clear mechanism to delete all data a company holds on them, with narrow exceptions for legal obligations, legal claims, and fraud or security purposes.

Publicly traded companies would have to disclose the aggregate value of the user data they hold, revenue from collecting and selling user data, contracts over $10 million to collect or license data, and acquisitions of user data valued above $100 million.
Violations of the user-facing requirements would be treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act and enforced by the FTC.

analysis.who_pays: The largest internet companies and data brokers, which would bear compliance costs, lose a measure of opacity around how they monetize user data, and could see investors and users scrutinize that revenue stream more closely.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech platforms and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The 100-million-user threshold exempts smaller companies and data brokers below that line, leaving much of the data-broker market outside the bill's reach.

Requiring companies to assign and report a dollar value to each user's data every 90 days is administratively difficult, and the bill's valuation methods would have to be invented by regulators from scratch, raising questions about accuracy and comparability.

The deletion right includes exceptions for legal obligations, legal claims, and fraud prevention, and requires companies to retain no more data than those exceptions require — limits that advocates of stronger privacy laws would call incomplete.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The user-facing transparency and deletion rights are real, meaningful protections at essentially no direct cost to consumers; the main honest objections are the arbitrary 100-million-user threshold and the difficulty of valuing data on a fixed schedule. On balance a net gain for ordinary users, with the burden falling on the companies that profit from the data.

outcome.mechanism: After being introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee in June 2019, the bill's only action was a committee hearing in October 2019; the committee never marked it up or brought it to the floor before Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Mark Warner (D-VA) introduced the bill on June 25, 2019, joined by Sen. Josh Hawley (R-MO), giving it bipartisan sponsorship.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The committee held a hearing on the bill on October 24, 2019 (S.Hrg. 116-182), but took no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill died without ever receiving a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large internet platforms and data brokers — they avoided new disclosure, deletion, and valuation requirements, and kept the current opacity around how they monetize user data. Investors likewise never got the standardized data-value disclosures.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan — a Democratic sponsor and one Republican cosponsor — but died in committee, so the chamber never took a party-line vote; no floor or committee vote exists to measure party positions.

industries.industry: Large online platforms (social media, search, and consumer internet services)
industries.note: Companies with over 100 million U.S. users would have had to reveal what data they collect and how they use it, tell users what their data is worth, let users delete it, and disclose data revenue to investors. Their business depends on monetizing user data with limited visibility, so the bill's gain for transparency is their cost.

Firms that collect, process, sell, or share consumer data at scale would face the same disclosure, deletion, and valuation requirements. A deletion right and public disclosure of data revenue directly cut into a market built on trading personal information without consumer visibility.

Publicly traded data companies would have had to disclose the aggregate value of user data held, data-related revenue, and major third-party data contracts, giving investors a standard way to see how much of a company's business rests on user data.
